title: Practice, Data and Sim Racing
intro: Drivers get faster by practising with a purpose and by measuring what they do. This page covers how to practise, how to read lap times and telemetry, and how to set up a driving simulator or racing game so that it trains the right habits. Professional drivers use simulators to learn tracks before they race on them, and sim racers use the same data tools as race engineers.

items: Learn a track in stages: first the direction of every corner and where the track goes; then the line and the reference points; then the braking points; only then the limit.
Work on one thing per run: braking later into one corner, or carrying more speed through one sweeper. Trying to fix everything at once fixes nothing.

Use the sectors. Tracks are timed in sectors (often three), so a driver can see which part of the lap is slow. Adding up the best time of each sector gives a theoretical best (ideal) lap, which shows how much time is available without any new skill.
Use a ghost or reference lap. Many games can show a ghost car of your best lap or of a faster driver's lap; following it shows where they brake, turn in and get on the throttle.
Long runs as well as single laps. A race needs consistent laps on worn tyres and in traffic, not one perfect lap on new tyres.
Stop when tired. Late in a long session, mistakes rise and the lessons get worse.

blocks.text: Telemetry is the record of what the car did, sampled many times a second: speed, throttle and brake position, steering angle, gear, engine speed, lateral and longitudinal acceleration, and often tyre temperatures and suspension travel. Real teams log it from sensors on the car; most simulators can export it to analysis tools. The most useful view plots two laps against distance round the lap, one over the other, so that differences line up.

items: Speed trace: the lowest speed in each corner (minimum speed) and the speed at the end of each straight. A higher speed at the end of a straight usually means a better exit from the corner before it, not a stronger engine.
Brake trace: a fast lap shows a sharp rise to peak pressure and a smooth taper into the corner (trail braking). A slow lap often shows a slow rise, a flat plateau and an abrupt release.

Throttle trace: look for the point of first throttle and the point of full throttle. Hesitation, a dip, or on-off-on in the middle of a corner shows where the driver lacked confidence or the car lacked balance.
Steering trace: smooth single arcs are good; saw-tooth corrections show slides. An understeering car shows a lot of lock with little extra turning; a counter-steer spike shows oversteer.

Time delta: a running plot of how far ahead or behind the reference lap the driver is. Where it climbs steeply is where the time is lost, which is often before the corner in question (a poor entry costs on the straight that follows).

blocks.text: Compare against a lap that is only a little faster. A lap three seconds faster differs everywhere at once and teaches little; one that is three tenths faster shows exactly which corners to work on.

items: Wheel and pedals: a steering wheel with force feedback and a set of pedals, firmly mounted to a desk, stand or cockpit that does not move. A load-cell brake pedal measures force rather than travel, as a real brake does, and makes threshold braking much more repeatable.

Force feedback: the wheel motor reproduces the forces the front tyres send up the steering column. It is the main way a sim driver feels grip, so set it strong enough to feel the steering go light at the limit, but not so strong that it clips (hits its maximum and goes flat, hiding the detail).

Steering ratio and rotation: match the wheel's rotation to the car's real steering lock (for example 540 or 900 degrees lock to lock), so that the wheel in the hands turns the same amount as the virtual one.

Field of view: the angle of the scene shown should match the angle the screen covers from the driver's eye, so speeds and distances look true. The vertical angle is $\theta = 2 \arctan\left(\frac{h}{2d}\right)$ for a screen of height $h$ at distance $d$. A 27 inch 16:9 monitor (about 34 cm tall) at 60 cm gives about 31 degrees, much less than most games' default, so the default view often makes the car feel slower than it is.
Frame rate and input lag: a high, steady frame rate and low display lag make the car easier to catch in a slide, because the picture of the rotation arrives sooner.
Seating: sit as in a car, with knees slightly bent and arms slightly bent at the wheel. A comfortable, solid position gives consistent inputs.

blocks.text: Games offer aids that make a car easier to drive. Some, such as ABS and traction control, are allowed in many real racing series and are part of the car. Others, such as stability control (which brakes individual wheels to stop slides), automatic braking, steering assistance and a drawn-on racing line, are teaching aids. A useful path is to start with aids on, learn the tracks, then turn them off one at a time, starting with the racing line, and relearn the braking points without it. Driving without an aid is not automatically faster: modern traction control and ABS are often as fast as a skilled driver, but learning without them teaches what the tyres are doing.
What carries over between games and real cars

items: Carries over well: track knowledge, the line, reference points, braking points (in a good sim), racecraft, the logic of setup and the reading of data.
Carries over partly: car control and the feel of the limit. A sim teaches the right responses but not the physical sensations of grip, which a real driver learns through the seat.
Does not carry over: the physical demand (neck and core strength against high g, heat in the cockpit) and the fear factor of a real accident.
Many professional drivers train on simulators, and several sim racers have moved into real racing, because the skills of consistency, smoothness and racecraft are the same.

blocks.text: Sources: Segers, J. (2014), Analysis Techniques for Racecar Data Acquisition, 2nd ed., SAE International. Smith, C. (1996), Drive to Win, Carroll Smith Consulting, on practice and testing. Bentley, R. (1998), Speed Secrets, Motorbooks.
